metadata.file_name: Exploring school factors related to professional learning communities  a machine learning approach using cross-national data.pdf
metadata.title: Exploring school factors related to professional learning communities: a machine learning approach using cross-national data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 school-level data (main population ISCED level 2) pooled across 42 countries/economies, with a two-stage sampling design (randomly sampled schools, then random teachers within schools). The authors construct a school-level PLC dependent variable from teacher responses and then train supervised ML models on predictors from the TALIS 2018 principal questionnaire. The manuscript does not report applying TALIS sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation, and the ML pipeline (KNN imputation, scaling, and XGBoost/RF/LASSO/Ridge/CART) is described without any weight-aware estimation. Given the absence of explicit weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and the lack of discussion of complex survey design in the ML stage, the analysis is treated as unweighted; this may affect generalizability and uncertainty quantification under TALIS’s clustered sampling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 data for the main population at ISCED level 2. The dependent variable (PLC) was created at the school level from teacher responses using a composite measure with three subdimensions and 14 items (Table 1). From the principal questionnaire, the authors excluded 14 question batteries (108 items) that were only administered conditionally (filtered items) to avoid imputing irrelevant responses. They further excluded one battery of four items where each item had >12% missing data, and excluded an additional battery of 11 items because they were very similar to teacher-level items already used to construct the PLC measure (to avoid overlap between dependent and independent variables). The remaining dataset was split into training (75%) and test (25%) sets with stratification on the PLC variable; missing values in both sets were imputed using KNN with k selected via parameter sweep (odd k from 1 to 19), choosing k=7 based on MAE/MSE/RMSE trade-offs.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Years willing to continue as principal

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (ISCED level 2), school-level PLC measure (42 countries/economies)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison on test data: XGBoost — RMSE: 0.097, RSQ: 0.294; CART — RMSE: 0.109, RSQ: 0.112; LASSO — RMSE: 0.099, RSQ: 0.275; Random forest — RMSE: 0.100, RSQ: 0.269; Ridge — RMSE: 0.099, RSQ: 0.276. Variable importance interpreted using XGBoost gain; relationships further visualized with ALE plots.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (ISCED level 2) the study leveraged school administrative staffing, number of teachers, school location, staff support satisfaction, and instructional leadership feedback to predict school-level PLC levels, finding that XGBoost achieved the lowest test RMSE (0.097) and highest test RSQ (0.294) among five compared algorithms. This indicates that PLC functioning is strongly associated with actionable school- and leadership-level conditions (e.g., staffing structure and instructional leadership practices), suggesting that policy and school improvement efforts should target leadership feedback routines and supportive resourcing rather than treating PLCs as purely culture-driven, while noting the study is exploratory and does not make causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses TALIS 2018 cross-national data for the main population at ISCED level 2, constructing a school-level Professional Learning Communities (PLC) dependent variable from teacher responses (three subdimensions, 14 items). Using 42 countries/economies and a supervised ML pipeline, the authors compare five regression algorithms (CART, LASSO, Ridge, Random Forest, XGBoost) with 75/25 stratified train/test splitting on the PLC variable. Missing values are imputed with KNN (k selected via sweep 1–19; best k=7), and predictors are preprocessed via dummy coding for nominal variables, removal of non-varying predictors, and standardization. On the test set, XGBoost outperforms alternatives with RMSE=0.097 and RSQ=0.294 (vs. CART RMSE=0.109, RSQ=0.112; others RMSE≈0.099–0.100, RSQ≈0.269–0.276). The paper is explicitly exploratory and does not incorporate TALIS complex-survey weighting in the ML stage, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript reports the total number of schools (8128) and that the PLC measure is school-level, but it does not provide a student-level analytic N, nor does it list per-country sample sizes in the provided text. Therefore, total_students and countries/n_students cannot be populated from the excerpt without additional tables (e.g., Appendix 1 or a sample characteristics table).
